cultivar: Yibang small-leaf population (xiaoyezhong), grown alongside ordinary Yunnan large-leaf trees
processing: Raw pu-erh: pan-fired, hand-rolled and sun-dried maocha pressed into cakes; the small, tender leaf is fired lightly and rolled gently to avoid breaking.
harvest_season: Spring (late March to April) is the harvest the reputation rests on; autumn tea is softer and cheaper.
appearance_dry: Noticeably small, slim, dark-green leaves with small tight buds, looking almost like a green tea next to a Bulang cake.
appearance_wet: Small, neat, tender yellow-green leaves, much finer than typical pu-erh material.
taste_profile: Refined and aromatic: honey, orchid and a light fruitiness, a fine bitterness that fades quickly, some gentle astringency, a light-to-medium body and a long, clear, sweet aftertaste.

brewing.notes: Rinse once, briefly. The small leaf gives up its flavour fast, so flash the first steeps; porcelain and water just off the boil keep the aroma clean.

vintage_note: Sold by spring harvest year and by sub-area (Mansong, Malishu, Daheishulin, Mangong, Yibang old street), mostly as small-run cakes and maocha from boutique producers since the mid-2000s, when the six ancient mountains came back into fashion. Young (1–3 years) Yibang is perfumed and fine; it fills out into honey over the 5–12-year window, and aged Yibang in the real sense is almost unobtainable because the mountain produced little under its own name before 2005. Supply is 2005–2025, dry-stored, and prices for old-tree small-leaf tea are high while the newer large-leaf plantings around the villages are much cheaper.
description:
Yibang is one of the six ancient tea mountains of Xishuangbanna, in Xiangming township of Mengla County, and it was the administrative and trading centre of the Qing-era tea trade before Yiwu took over; the old cobbled street and the tea-merchant ruins are still there. Its tea is unusual in Yunnan because much of it comes from a small-leaf population, said locally to have been brought by Sichuan merchants, which gives a finer, more perfumed cup than big-leaf pu-erh.

The old gardens are scattered through forest at around 1,300–1,500 m, interplanted with ordinary large-leaf trees, and the tribute village of Mansong is part of the Yibang area. Processing is ordinary sheng, but the small, tender leaf has to be fired and rolled gently, and the pressed cakes look strikingly fine-grained.

In the cup, Yibang is honey and orchid with a light fruitiness, a quick fine bitterness, a little astringency and a long clear sweetness; the body is lighter than Yiwu's, but the aftertaste is persistent. It gives up its flavour quickly, so short early steeps matter more here than anywhere. People who brew it like a Bulang find it thin and sharp; people who brew it with care find it one of the most elegant teas in Yunnan.

Sold by spring year and sub-area, and the names carry real price differences, with Mansong at the top and old-street Yibang gushu not far behind. Because the mountain lost many old trees to fires and clearance in the twentieth century, genuine old-tree small-leaf tea is scarce, and much 'Yibang' is young planting or large-leaf material from the surrounding slopes. Small leaf size is the quickest visual check.

It is a good tea to drink alongside Yiwu: the same honeyed region expressed in a finer, higher key.
history:
Yibang is one of the six ancient tea mountains of Xishuangbanna, in Xiangming township of Mengla County. In the Qing period it was an important centre of the regional tea trade, and it is linked with the tribute tea of nearby Mansong.

The usual story says that Sichuan merchants brought the small-leaf tea plants that set Yibang apart, but that remains local tradition. The trade later shifted towards Yiwu, and the mountain's name returned to wide use with the revival of interest in the six ancient mountains.
